texts.facts: The accused Nos.1 and 2 in C.C.No.114 of 2002 on the files of the Chief Judicial Magistrate Court, Thodupuzha filed this Revision Petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 16(1A)(i), 2(ia)(f)(h) (j) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rules 29 and 44A of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 and Sections 16(i)(a)(ii) and 7(iii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 read with Rule 50(1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955. 2. Heard. 3. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- On 9.7.2002 at 12.30 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector, purchased two packets, each packet contained 250 gram of dal, from the shop of the first accused. The second accused was the licensee of the said shop and the third accused was the whole sale dealer of the food item. After sampling as per rules, one of the samples was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst. The Public Analyst filed Ext. P13 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for the food item under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 and therefore, the same was adulterated. Thereafter, on the request of the accused, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. Ext.P16 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would also show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for the food item and therefore, the same was adulterated. It was further alleged that the second accused sold the food item without having a valid licence under the PFA Rules. 4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW4 were examined and Exts. P1 to P24 series were marked for the prosecution. DW1 to DW4 were examined and Exts.D1 to D13 were marked for the revision petitioners.
texts.arguments: 5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P16 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated. The learned counsel for the revision Smt. Suma Rajan vs Food Inspector on 14 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/139202112/ 2 petitioners relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. 6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act. Therefore, Ext. P16 certificate of Central Food Laboratory cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra). It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
